utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I might, we have -- there are some issues to address with respect to the second witness who is going to testify today, MM-038. There are some issues, but could we go into private session to discuss those issues, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, we may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would call the next witness, Mr. Ante Marinovic. If he could be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please read out the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you understand me okay in your own language?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Not you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But do you understand what the interpreters are telling you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Is the volume in your headphones okay? If it's not, just speak up and we'll fix that, okay?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, if at any time you don't understand one of my questions, also please just say so and I'll try to state it more clearly. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Ante Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: In Bruska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's Bruska in Croatia, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In what year were you born?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Marinovic, you attended elementary school in Bruska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you later graduated from secondary school in Benkovac in 1977; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you perform military service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember in which years that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you subsequently work at the shoe factory in Benkovac until it closed in 1989?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was called Jugoplastika.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you become a reserve police officer in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when in 1991 you joined?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: In the spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what did that entail? What were your duties as a reserve police officer?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: To guard the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you have regular shifts to guard the village?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about weapons? Did you have weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you retire from the reserve police in 1996?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Because I was no longer fit to do that work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Why were you no longer fit to do that work?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Because I'm an invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just briefly, what do you mean? Why are you an invalid? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm unfit to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is it because of what happened to you, what you're about to testify to today?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you more about that later. But for now I'm going to ask you some questions about Bruska.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, to help you situate, Bruska is marked on map 8 of Exhibit 22, and you can also find it on page 25 of the atlas. It's towards the bottom of grid D2, Bruska and some of the other villages which will be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Marinovic, if you know, approximately how many people lived in Bruska in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: About 400, including men, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were the residents mostly Croats, Serbs or a mix?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: There were five Orthodox houses, so it was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And other than those five Orthodox houses, what ethnicity were the rest of the residents?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Could you also name for us some of the surrounding villages and tell us whether their residents were Croats, Serb or a mix?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can enumerate the villages: Medvidja, Zelengrad, Karin, Brgud, Bjeline, Kalanja Draga. Those were the villages around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Was Medvidja a Croat or a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Half-half.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about Zelengrad?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Karin?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Bjeline?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were about 20 per cent Croats there, and the rest were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Brgud?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned one other. What was the other village you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Zelengrad?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think we -- Valana --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Kalanja Draga.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. What was the ethnicity of that village?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just so it's clear, for everyone here, when you say "Orthodox," do you mean Serb?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Up until 1990, how would you characterise the relations between Croats and Serbs in Bruska and the surrounding area, the villages you've just named for us?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did those relations deteriorate at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: When the elections began.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember which year those elections were held?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Which political party won the elections in Bruska, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: The HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know which political party was favoured by the Serb residents in your area?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: The SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were only two parties who had candidates, so how could I not know?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you -- did anyone ever tell you that they supported the SDS, or did you ever see any posters or anything from the SDS that led you to believe that they had support in your area?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: There were posters all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. As you understood it, what were the political goals of the SDS? In your understanding.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Their political goals of the SDS was for all of that to be only Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marinovic. I won't ask you any more questions about politics.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Marinovic, did you or your neighbours own weapons in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about Serb residents in the area? Did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: The army distributed weapons to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When was that, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in the spring, early spring. They gave them weapons. I don't know exactly when. The army transported and distributed weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Spring of which year; 1990 or 1991, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And how did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the late Sveto told me about that - when they killed my father and brother, they killed him too - that they were distributing villages -- that they were distributing weapons in Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What is Sveto's surname?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Draca.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Marinovic, were you able to travel back and forth between Bruska and Benkovac in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, we were not. When we went to that Medvidja, there were barricades. There were people standing guard there. They didn't let us pass through, and then when we went to Benkovac, they stopped us, searched us, and there would be about ten of them with rifles in their hands, holding us at gunpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know who those people were or where they came from, the people who were manning the barricades?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Towards Medvidja, it was local people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what about in the direction of Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in the direction of Benkovac, I knew some of them and I didn't know others, so then the ones that I didn't know were probably from somewhere around Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember how these people were dressed, the people who were at the barricades?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms -- oh, the barricades. At Medvidja, they wore military uniforms. The olive-green-grey, whatever you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And at the barricades on the -- in the direction of Benkovac? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them wore camouflage uniforms, camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Moving to a slightly different topic now, are you familiar with a factory called Ponos which was located in Bruska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was that factory operational in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: It stopped working, I think, in 1991, or December of 1990, I don't know exactly. I wasn't working there. I only know about where I worked. I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember something that happened to the Ponos factory in May or June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I remember when some people came and started shooting, and there was a water tank there and they shot it -- shot at it and it was all bullet-riddled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know who those people were or where they came from, the ones who shot at the water tank?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I think they were probably people from Karin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know which ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Marinovic, you've now mentioned some barricades and an incident at Ponos factory. Did you ever see military vehicles in Bruska in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I saw military vehicles as they were moving towards Krusevo, and then they were -- well, shelling, bombing, whatever the word may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember about what time of the year, approximately, you saw those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the month of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What kind of vehicles did you see?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you be any more precise about what they looked like, what kinds of vehicles they were?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: They were TAM trucks, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. How far from Bruska is the village of Krusevo?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you take the road around, it would be 10 to 12 kilometres. If you take the shortcut on foot, then it would be about eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were its residents Croats, Serbs or a mix?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was shelling. Do you know where the shelling came from?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Medvidja and Zelengrad, that direction, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And do you know who conducted the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: The army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How do you know these things about Krusevo?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: How could I not know when all of this went through my village, towards Krusevo, that direction?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you actually able to see or hear any of the shelling of Krusevo?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. All of that could be heard in our village. If something is going on in Krusevo, you can hear it as if it were there, if you were there yourself. It's two or three kilometres only. You can hear everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me now ask you something about something slightly different. We've talked about vehicles. But did you see men in military uniforms in Bruska in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: In vehicles. People went in vehicles then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Were you able to see the people who were in those vehicles, what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you describe it? What kind of uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Military uniforms, green.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you already mentioned to us, you've told us about Krusevo. When was the first time that you remember seeing men in military uniforms in Bruska or passing through Bruska, as you described?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, right after the elections, 1991, they were passing by in military uniforms. They got weapons from the army and all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, you've described seeing people in what you call army uniforms. Did you ever see any -- anyone that you thought was a paramilitary as opposed to the army?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When did you first see such people in Bruska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: In Bruska, these local ones, I think it was those paramilitaries that went around scaring people, whereas these who were going to Krusevo from Benkovac, I cannot say that they were paramilitaries. I cannot say whether they were active or not. Perhaps they were some kind of military reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And -- I think you're distinguishing between some people who you think were paramilitaries and other people who were more military, maybe military reserve. Did you see those people together, or were they separate when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you see them on separate occasions?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, everybody came whenever they felt like it. Whenever they wanted to. For example, to my village, they would come to my village to scare people around, and they said, "You have no business here. This is Serb. You can go away."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Who was it who had come to your village and said things like that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, those from up there, from Medvidja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And when did they come, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I think that not two days would go by without them coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember anything else specific that they said or did besides saying that you had no business here, that this is Serb, you can go away?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how can I say? I mean, let me think what else I can remember. I just know that they came and that that's what they were saying to us, that we were Ustashas, that we had no business there, that that would be Greater Serbia, that we had no business there, that we should get our stuff and leave. That was their main point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: During 1991, did you or the other people in your village take any action to protect yourselves against these threats that you just described?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they took it. I mean, we had nothing. We did not have any weapons or anything. How can I do anything about it? I don't have any weapons or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What do you mean by "they took it. I mean, we had nothing." Just not sure I understand that.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Rifles, weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you mean that someone took the rifles and weapons? I'm not -- I don't understand this. Could you please explain this point to me.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No. They had weapons. We had nothing. So I cannot oppose them in any way then. How can I do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I think I understand. And when you say "they had weapons," who is "they"? Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: The people from Medvidja who kept coming to our village, those Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Marinovic, now I'm going to start asking you some questions about December 1991. First of all, how many of the inhabitants of Bruska were still living there in December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And where were you yourself on the evening of 21 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: At home.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who was with you at your home on that evening?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: It was me, my late brother, my late father, the late Sveto, my late uncle, and the children had gone to bed and my grandfather had gone to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, before I ask you what happened, let me just ask you a few questions about the people you just mentioned. First of all, what were you doing at home that evening?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: We were playing cards in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were any of you armed? Did you have weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. We did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How were you dressed?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Ordinary clothes, like this, the way we are usually dressed. Somebody had a jacket, whatever. How can I say what they wore?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Did -- was anyone wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, you testified earlier that you were a reserve policeman at the time. Were you active, on duty, that night, that evening?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you part of any military or paramilitary force?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about your brother and your father and Sveto? And your uncle?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were any of them members of a military or paramilitary force?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Marinovic, what was -- what were the ethnicity of the other people you mentioned? Were they all Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Sveto was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And were the other people -- your father and your brother and your uncle were all Croats, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Why was Sveto Draca at your house that evening?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Sveto and I grew up together. We went to school together. He was simply with us. What can I say? That's how we felt. We were together all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'm going to ask you to tell the Court what happened to you that evening, and we are going to go through it step by step. First of all, what time was it in the evening when this happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: 8, 8.30, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And what happened at 8 or 8.30?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: We were sitting at a table and playing cards. My late uncle sat near us and he was watching. Then three of them barged into the house. One of them was standing at the door of the house and the other two barged in and they immediately said, "Get up from that table." We got up and then they said, "Go out." And we were wondering what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few questions about the three of --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You said three of them barged into the house. What were those three people wearing?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you describe anything more about what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: On their sleeves, it said "Milicija Krajina," the Krajina Police. They were not masked, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know any of those three men or recognise them?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I recognised one of them but I didn't know his name or surname. I knew him from soccer football because I liked playing soccer football and there is not a single village in the area where I did not play soccer football. So I knew all the guys, Serbs and Croats, all who were involved in sports. I recognised him. I didn't know his name or surname -- oh, yes, I see. He was a goalie in one of the villages, in one of the clubs there. So then the pictures -- they took out the pictures of football players and put them in front of me and I recognised them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a couple of questions about what you just said. You talked about some pictures and they took out pictures. Who do you mean? Who took out pictures?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: That happened -- now, that was after the exchange. It was at the police station in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So that -- when did that happen; what year, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: 1993, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And was that when you learned the name of this person that you had recognised on the 21st of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question so that I understand it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sure. You've told us how you saw some pictures at the police station in 1993. Was that when you learned the name of the person who you recognised that night?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's when I found out what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after these three men barged in and told you to go outside, I want you to tell us what happened next. And please take your time and tell us what you remember.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that they took us out of the house and they lined us up against a wall, all of us, and when they started shooting, Sveto and my late Uncle Petar started running away. I, my brother and my father -- well, my father and my brother were killed, but then we all fell and now was somebody running after them and shooting or was somebody outside the yard and shooting them, I don't know, but they were killed at the gate in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Who shot at you? Was it the same people who had come into the house?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How many times were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Seven times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you tell us where on your body you were hit by the bullets?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Twice in the left thigh, or above the left thigh, twice in the arm, twice above the right hip, and once in the hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you remain conscious through all this or at some point did you lose consciousness?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I fell onto the ground. I don't know when I came to. Maybe it was five minutes later, 15 minutes later, ten minutes later, half an hour later; I don't know. I don't know when I came to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. When you came to, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw my late father and my late brother dead next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Then I went to the room and changed, and my sister-in-law walked out and said, What happened? And I said, Nothing, nothing. And I thought I had to leave. So when I left the yard, I saw Sveto and my late uncle dead by the gate, and then I went to Kalanja Draga through the woods. It's about six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And how did you get to Kalanja Draga?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: How? On foot. Barefoot. Half of the trip I made in one trainer only but then I didn't dare take it off although it was full of blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived in Kalanja Draga?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: We had some relatives there and I went to stay with them and they took me in and they called an emergency -- or rather, they called an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And did the ambulance come for you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Where did it take you first?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: To Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you receive any kind of medical treatment in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They dressed my wounds and later on I sort of -- well, went the other way. I wasn't really myself any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. After you were -- after they dressed your wounds in Benkovac, were you taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They took me to Knin, to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember how you got to the hospital in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember how I got there. I just know that -- well, I remember it through a haze because I had bled so much, and I don't remember all of that. I don't remember how I got to the hospital in Knin. I really cannot remember all of that. I will tell you what I know, and what I don't know, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So do you remember, on the way to Knin, being interviewed or interrogated by anybody?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Once you reached the hospital in Knin, did you undergo any kind of medical procedure there?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember any of that, but later on, when I came to in hospital, I saw that they did all of this properly. The doctors were very fair. I have nothing to say against them. Especially this man Dr. Ignjatovic, I think that he works at the military medical hospital, and he is a really good doctor, very fair. I have nothing bad to say about him. On the contrary, if I would ever see him, I would buy him a treat. They were so good to me. There is nothing I can say about them that would be bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the hospital, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was nine or ten or 11 days. I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: While you were there in the hospital, do you remember anyone threatening or insulting you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you describe to us what happened on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: When I was in my room, somebody came in, this one man, maybe a friend brought him in or something, I don't know, then he saw me and then this Dr. Ignjatovic was there, and this man who came in said, "This Ustasha should be slaughtered immediately." And Dr. Ignjatovic said, "Leave, sir, leave straight away. I have work to do in this hospital and you do not belong here. You belong outside."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This person who came in and said, "This Ustasha should be slaughtered immediately," do you remember what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you remember anything else? Did he have any insignia or anything on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Milicija Krajina, the Krajina Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you were released from the hospital, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I went to see my sister-in-law. She was a Serb too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember if you went back to Bruska before you went to see your sister-in-law?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Later on I went to Bruska, after one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us about that time when you went back to Bruska, then. And just tell us what you remember about it.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: When I got back to Bruska, I'll tell you what I remember. I found my aunt and uncle there. They had survived. And I stayed with them, and then my sister and brother-in-law came, and another man, called Nikola. I think his last name was Dragosavac. My sister had married a Serb in Lika, the village of Vrebac. They stayed with us for a while and then they told me to go with them, so I went to the village of Vrebac in Lika with them. I spent less than two hours in Bruska on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So just one more question about that occasion: Do you remember who travelled with you back to Bruska from Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: From Knin to Bruska, I went to Benkovac, and then from Benkovac to Bruska, and somebody gave me a lift. His last name was Burza. I can't remember his first name now. He drove me to Bruska. I think he was some kind of police inspector. He was a very good man. He treated me very fairly. I can say nothing bad about him. I don't want to say bad things about anybody. I will only speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, returning for a moment to the 21st of December 1991, when you were shot and what you've described to us, other than your family -- your brother and your father and your uncle and Sveto Draca, did you learn whether anyone else was killed in Bruska on that evening?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I learned that in the hospital in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What did you learn?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: That they had killed Ika Marinovic, Dragan Marinovic, Stana Marinovic, Manda Marinovic, Krste Marinovic, and Draginja Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember from whom you learned this?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I do. It was the mother of Jasna who had been wounded and was in the hospital in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know Jasna's surname, the one she uses now?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: The one she uses now is Denona.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And these people you mentioned, Ika, Dragan, Stana, Manda, Krste and Draginja Marinovic, do you know anything about what happened to their bodies?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there, I only heard about it; that they took them to the local cemetery and buried them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you hear anything more about what happened to them years later, after they were buried?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Later? Later, Oso Marinovic was killed, I don't know when. And in 1996, after Operation Storm, we exhumed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. What about the other people that you mentioned? Do you know if they were ever exhumed?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Marinovic, why do you think that you and your family and your co-villagers were attacked in this way? Why did these people try to kill you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Only because we were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Marinovic, I'm almost done with my questions. I just have a few more short topics and then the Defence may have some questions for you. Do you remember ever giving a statement to the Serb police about what happened to you in Bruska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about to the Croatian authorities? Do you remember ever giving a statement to them?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I did, in Zadar, I think. I gave them a statement. When I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Any -- can you recall what year that was or the approximate date?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 1993, towards the end of the year, but I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Focusing on the Serb authorities, do you know if anyone was ever prosecuted by the Serb authorities for what happened in Bruska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about the Serb police investigating those crimes?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Marinovic, after the events which you've described to us today, including the brief return to Bruska after you were released from the hospital, after all of that, when was the next time you were able to return to Bruska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: The first time was on the 6th of August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what did you find there in Bruska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I found the house full of ammunition, about 60 or 70 truckloads of ammunition. That's what I found in the hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What condition were the houses in, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: The windows and the door frames had been taken away. It was all broken. I had to make a door to prevent the rain falling in. There was nothing there. Everything was wrecked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, finally, Mr. Marinovic, do you currently suffer any physical effects from the gunshot wounds which you received on the 21st of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I have very serious consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what those consequences are, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly when the weather is changing, everything hurts. I can't even walk or move my arm. I have a severe pain in my leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did these wounds prevent you from working?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the co-counsel, Nikola Perovic, will conduct the cross-examination. We can either begin now and then have a break in five minutes, but if the Chamber feels this is a convenient time, we could start after the break. It's up to the Chamber to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe let's start now and break in five minutes' time. Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I assume you understand I am a member of the Defence team for Mr. Martic. I am Nikola Perovic and I will cross-examine you according to the Rules of Procedure. You used to be a shoemaker, as you said, in a factory which stopped working in 1989; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After that, you said you joined the police units, the reserve police units.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't immediately. It was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What year was it in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt? I think the interpreter is having difficulty keeping pace. If you can just slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I was about to ask you that. As we understand each other, could you please make a short pause before you begin answering my questions so the interpreters can do their job. So in 1990 or 1991, you joined the reserve police forces?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Were these regular police forces or para-police forces?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: There were no para-police forces. What para-police forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because you said you had no uniform or weapons.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have that, because we couldn't get that. All of Croatia didn't have any weapons or uniforms at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, in 1991, did you have occasion to see men who were neither soldiers nor policemen and who put on uniforms of any sort?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: What men are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, generally in those days.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw the Serbs from Medvidja a million times. They would put on those clothes and come to maltreat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, they were neither soldiers nor policemen yet they put on uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: They said they were Martic's police, "Martica Milicija." That's what they said. How true that was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say in your statement that in 1990 there were no weapons in Bruska.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And that the army armed the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Sveto told us the army was transporting weapons up there. Sveto, who was killed, told us this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Sveto Draca?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: But you did not mention him as the source of your information when you made your statement in the year 2000 to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe they didn't ask me, or you didn't ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have an opportunity, but maybe the investigators did.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but they probably didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So you remember this later on?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that interview. I can't remember what happened yesterday, let alone 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. Court adjourned. We will come back at quarter to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marinovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said that the relations between the Serbs and the Croats up to 1990 were correct.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Those relations deteriorated in connection with the elections that took place in 1990. That's what you explained, right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And you said in that context that Bruska strongly supported the HDZ. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were Croats so who else would they support, that Croatia should be Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify this?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, be more precise.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be more precise. I've explained what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll put the question in the following way --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: You can put it any way you like but I know what I'm going to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the HDZ, were there any other Croatian parties participating in the elections?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: The SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Croatian parties?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no Croatian parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was the Party of Democratic Change a Croatian party participating in the elections?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Serbs wanted their own state without any Croats in it, right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: My question about this is the following: What did the Croats who voted for the HDZ want?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: What the Croats wanted? They had the right to their nationhood, just as the Serbs did. Just as there was a state of Serbia, so the same obtained in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the Croats wanted their own state?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: I was never involved in politics. I was never active in politics. Nor am I active in politics now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: But you said that the Serbs wanted their -- their state.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if they hadn't wanted that, they wouldn't have done what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And I asked you what the Croats wanted.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Croats wanted Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be a pause between question and answer. The interpreters did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, can you please slow down? The interpreters says she couldn't hear the answer from the witness. The question was: "The Croatian state?" How do you answer to that, Mr. Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the Croats wanted? They wanted Croatia to be Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that military vehicles often passed through Bruska, especially during the attack on Krusevo.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Were these vehicles belonging to the then-JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And this was at a time when the JNA was the only regular armed force in the country; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "regular"? Where was the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was the summer of 1991, Mr. Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have told you that the army went to shell and bomb Krusevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Why Krusevo? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Because it was a Croatian village. They wanted to take Zadar but they were not successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How long did this attack on Krusevo go on?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what do I know? I can't be precise. Four, five, seven, eight days. I don't know exactly how long the attack on Krusevo lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the investigators, you said that the shelling of Krusevo lasted for about two months.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that. I might have done but I don't remember. All I know is that they went to shell Krusevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You don't know of any special reason why Krusevo was chosen of all places?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say that in September 1991, Krusevo was occupied and that the army stopped passing through Bruska, practically.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And that in the period from September until December 1991, in Bruska and the surrounding area, nothing significant happened.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And you also say that members of paramilitary units would come to the village and provoke you.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "members of paramilitary units," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: They were paramilitary units in the Krajina. They were all paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, to put my question more precisely, were these the people you mentioned as the people from Medvidja who put on uniforms without being either policemen or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Those people from Medvidja would come almost every day. They were dressed and they said they were the Krajina Police and that they were Martic's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That's what they said?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But whether they were paramilitary or military, I don't know; I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: We are now coming to the 21st of December 1991. In answer to the questions of the Prosecutor and before that, when interviewed by the investigators, you explained what happened on that evening.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And you said you were at home with your father, brother, uncle.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was my uncle on my mother's side, not my uncle on my father's side.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: These are two different words in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how Sveto Draca was dressed that evening?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: He was wearing normal clothes, like the ones I have on now. As far as I can recall. That's how I see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because witness Jasna Denona told us that on that evening he was wearing a uniform of a reserve JNA member.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say that. I don't recall that, because he came to see us every day. We were always together. I almost never saw him in that uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you don't exclude the possibility that he was wearing the uniform of a reservist. You say maybe you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that. I simply cannot recall that. I see him in my mind dressed the way I am dressed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And then three men, Martic's men, as you say, burst into your house.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say Martic's men. I said the Krajina policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you made to the investigators, which I can show you, it says: "Three of Martic's men broke into our house."

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I may have said that but I don't recall saying it, no. I said that three men burst in and that on their sleeves it said, "Krajina Police." "Milicija Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And it was based on those uniforms and insignia that you concluded they were members of the Krajina Police?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, you said there were people who put on different uniforms without being members of either the army or the police.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I saw at the time. I can't tell you anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, maybe let me -- Mr. Black is going to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I was just going to say that that mischaracterised your evidence, Your Honour. Counsel has put that to him several times but the witness has not adopted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I was going to say to you, Mr. Perovic. I've heard you say to this witness several times, you say -- "Do I understand you to say that people wore uniforms without being police?" How would he know that? I don't remember him ever saying so. This is what you have put to him. If people are wearing a uniform and it's written a name, the assumption is that they are those police. Unless he knows them and he can say, "I know you're not a policeman and I know you are not supposed to be wearing that police uniform."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You recognised one of them?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: His appearance; you didn't know his name.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: As what happened happened, you explained the circumstances under which you went to Bjeline or Kalanja Draga.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Kalanja Draga.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: To stay with Serb relatives.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mirko Kalanja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That was a friendship going back dozens of years?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And you consider those people relatives?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were my relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at their place, who called the ambulance among them?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be sure, but there was Kosa, Nikica Kalanja's wife, the daughter of Mirko. I think it was her.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Kosa Kalanja?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The daughter-in-law of Mirko Kalanja?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how she got word to the ambulance?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: They didn't have a telephone in their house?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How long did it take for the ambulance to arrive?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some 20 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just before the ambulance arrived, or about the same time, did some people in uniform come to the Kalanja house?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure or you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure. I'll tell you what I know. Don't ask me to say something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Marinovic, I expect you to tell me the truth and I'm sure that you're only telling me the truth and what you know.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I am just telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you that because in your statement to the police of Zadar, you mentioned some ten members of the army and you talked about olive-green-grey uniforms, and they came, you said, and you recognised Pajo Popovac [phoen] among them.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: He came with the emergency team, with the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Oh, alone or with somebody else in uniform?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I only knew Pajo among the men who came. Pajo is a very nice guy. He always treated me very nicely. I can only say good things about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: These uniforms that they wore, were they military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How did those uniformed men behave towards you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Very nicely. I cannot say anything that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The ambulance took to you Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After that, after you were given first aid, you were transferred to the Knin hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by then I had bled heavily, I don't remember this, I don't remember how I got to hospital, I cannot recall any of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Then I'm not going to insist on details, whether you remember who was with you in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I really don't know any of that. I really don't. Possibly someone was there, but I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Marinovic, will you please wait a little bit after the counsel has asked you your question to give time for the interpreter to interpret, then answer. Take it slow and don't push too hard too, Mr. -- Well, don't be too fast, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You had surgery in the Knin hospital --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Let me just finish. Please let me finish the question.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You stayed there for 15 days, you said that on one occasion, some man of Martic's came.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say a man of Martic's. I said that it said the Krajina Police. I didn't say one of Martic's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm reading your statement.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I know what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That man threatened you and said that you should be slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Why did that man come to hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did he come to visit someone and did he see you there by accident?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You talked about the way the doctors and medical staff treated you and you said that you were treated fairly.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Very fairly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I assume - and correct me if I'm wrong - that the medical staff were of Serb ethnicity for the most part.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When you were released from hospital, who drove you to Dobropoljci or --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: The bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How did you go to Bruska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I took the bus to Benkovac and then from Benkovac I was taken by Burza. He was a police inspector in Benkovac. I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Is it Milan Burza?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know his first name but I know his last name. So I don't know. I really don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was he a police inspector in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: A Serb?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And whose car did he take you in to Bruska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: His own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: His own private car?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then your sister came soon, Mirjan, was that her name?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, what's her name?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Ljubica. And Nikola Popovic, my brother-in-law, and Dragosavac, who was his friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Those two, Popovic and Dragosavac, what are they by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: They took you to Vrebac, near Medak.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Where they lived.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And how much time did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, almost a year. I left on the 17th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: At one point, you say that this was a village that was all under arms, that your brother-in-law was in uniform too.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: During that year, did you have any kind of trouble? Was there anything unpleasant that happened to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After Operation Storm in 1995, you returned to Bruska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In what kind of shape were the houses in Bruska when you came?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Very bad shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the investigators, you say, and I quote, "The houses were in pretty good shape. Only the windows and doors were broken."

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what can I say? When there is no windows and doors, then it's broken up, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So that's your statement?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So the houses were in good shape but there were no doors and windows?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how can you call that good shape, good condition, if there are no windows and doors?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said that you do not recall whether you talked to the police in Benkovac about what happened in Bruska.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I don't think so. I cannot remember any such thing. I don't remember having done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember or do you not remember or do you preclude that possibility altogether?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I preclude that possibility altogether. I never talked about that when I was there in Benkovac. I never talked about happened in Bruska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And in hospital, did any of the Serb police talk to you about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When you returned to Zadar, at the Zadar police in December 1992, you gave a statement about what had happened in Bruska.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Later on, you were heard before a military court in Split as a witness.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: No. That's a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This is the statement of Ante Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I was never in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Military court in Split, but you were heard in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a different ball game, but I was not in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This was November 1994. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was there a few times. When that happened exactly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If you do not remember, let me not insist.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In conclusion, just one question.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: During these almost 15 years that went by since 1992, since you gave your statement to the Croatian police, did Croatian military -- or rather, judicial and police authorities find the perpetrators in Bruska and punish them appropriately? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Marinovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded my cross-examination of Mr. Marinovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You mentioned your injuries and there was an injury to your hand. Could you indicate where.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: My arm. I can show it to you here, right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please do show it to us.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates] That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And you also mentioned more than one injury to your left thigh. And also to your right thigh? I do not think you will want to --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: The left, above my left thigh, in the groin. But it's only on the left, not on the right. On the right side, I have this, you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could we see what you're just disclosing? Could you stand up, possibly?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: And up here, up here. Here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could you indicate, turn around, so the Defence could see properly?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I can, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any other injuries?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: That you have not shown?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Twice in the groin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Here, in two places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Marinovic, I also have a few questions for you. You mentioned that the village of Krusevo was shelled. Was it the only village that was shelled during this period that you talked about today, or were there other villages?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Only in that period? Well, I don't know about further away, but that was the only village in our parts in that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Krusevo.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You also told us that your own home in Bruska had no door frames and window frames when you returned to it in 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were there other homes in Bruska that were also in bad shape?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The whole village?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the whole village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to give, in very general terms, a description of the damage that you observed in that whole village, on the homes?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I can just say what I saw. One of the hamlets was completely blown up. My hamlet of Marinovici, there weren't any doors or windows there. There were some roofs. And the houses were full of ammunition. And they tried to mend this, put some kind of makeshift doors. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said something about roofs. You said -- are you saying that these houses did or did not have roofs?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: There were roofs because there was ammunition inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But all the houses were damaged in one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know whose ammunition this was that you found in the houses?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Captain Dragan had his training grounds there in Bruska. He was training these special units there, sort of, of the Krajina. Well, I am telling you now what I actually know. It was big training grounds, and there was the Ponos factory, there was a school, and that was where they were, where this special police of theirs was. That's the only thing I know, so that's where the training grounds were and that's where they were training. And this training -- or rather, our hamlet was their ammunitions depot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And were you able to gain possession of your hamlet, notwithstanding the presence of ammunition inside?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Only one day later the Croatian police came, and they didn't let anyone in until the ammunition was taken away. This was after Operation Storm, after the liberation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You told us of the events of the day your father and other relatives were killed. Do you know if any other people in Bruska were killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In Krusevo, do you know whether any people were killed there?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know the state of the houses in Krusevo after the village had been shelled?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I was not there, and -- but from what I could see on pictures, they were all destroyed and burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate how big the village of Krusevo was?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: It was a very big village, Krusevo. I don't know what the population was, but it's a very big village. I think it had about 300 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mentioned in your evidence-in-chief that you exhumed a person by the name of Osmo Marinovic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Josip Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Josip Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any relation of yours?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How were you related?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we are close relatives. I don't know how to explain this to you. Cousins thrice removed, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. What are TAM trucks or T-A-M trucks?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You talked about military vehicles moving towards Krusevo, bombing and shelling, and you mentioned -- you called them TAM trucks, or at least that's what I saw on the transcript here: Capital T, capital A, capital M trucks.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.
